case.case_title: Premachandra v. Major Montague Jayawickrema and Another (Provincial Governors’ Case)
case.source_citation: Sri Lanka Law Reports [1994] 2 Sri LR. Supreme Court Reference Nos. 2/93 & 3/93, 4/93 & 5/93, decided on 16 August 1993

clause.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the appointment of Chief Ministers by Provincial Governors under Article 154F(4) infringed the fundamental right to equality before the law and equal protection under Article 12(1) of the Constitution.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The Petitioners argued that the Governors' appointment of UNP contenders as Chief Ministers, despite rival claims supported by evidence of majority support, infringed their fundamental rights under Article 12(1) by denying them equal protection of the law.
case_context.respondent_argument: The Respondents contended that the Governor's discretion under Article 154F(4) was subject to judicial review only on limited grounds and that the appointment did not infringe fundamental rights. They also argued that the Court of Appeal erred in referring only the question of infringement under Article 126(3) without proper hearing.
key_facts: Provincial Council elections held on 17.5.93 resulted in no absolute majority in North-Western and Southern Provinces.
Governors appointed UNP candidates as Chief Ministers despite Petitioners' claims of majority support.
Petitioners filed writ applications challenging the appointments and sought judicial review.
Court of Appeal referred only the question of infringement of fundamental rights under Article 126(3) without full hearing.
Supreme Court held that the reference under Article 126(3) was improper and only the reference under Article 125 was valid.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The Court held that Article 12(1) guarantees equality before the law and equal protection, which includes protection against arbitrary or discriminatory exercise of constitutional powers. The Governor's discretion under Article 154F(4) is subject to judicial review to ensure it is exercised lawfully, reasonably, and without improper considerations. The Court emphasized that no power is unfettered and all public powers must be exercised within legal limits consistent with the rule of law.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The Court found that the Petitioners had a constitutional right to the proper exercise of the Governor's power to appoint the Chief Minister. The Governor's decision must be based on objective evidence of majority support and not on irrelevant or improper considerations. The Court rejected the notion that the Governor's discretion was purely subjective or immune from review, thus protecting the Petitioners' right to equal protection under Article 12(1).
principles_established: All public powers, including constitutional discretions, are subject to legal limits and judicial review.
The rule of law prohibits unfettered discretion in public law.
Judicial review protects constitutional rights including equality before the law.
The Governor's discretion must be exercised for the public good and not for personal or political reasons.
Judicial review can be invoked if the Governor's decision is unreasonable, made in bad faith, or based on irrelevant considerations.

outcome.holding: The Court held that the Governor's discretion under Article 154F(4) is subject to judicial review and must be exercised lawfully and reasonably. The appointment of Chief Ministers is justiciable and the Petitioners' rights under Article 12(1) to equality before the law and equal protection are protected. The improper reference under Article 126(3) was rejected and the matter was remitted to the Court of Appeal for determination consistent with this ruling.
outcome.remedy_or_orders: Case sent back to the Court of Appeal with determination of the Supreme Court.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 12(1) is central to the Court's reasoning as it guarantees equality before the law and equal protection, which the Petitioners claimed was infringed by the Governor's appointment decisions. The Court's holding that the Governor's discretion is subject to judicial review protects this fundamental right.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The Court emphasized that no power is unfettered and all public powers must be exercised within legal limits consistent with the rule of law, protecting constitutional rights including equality before the law.
